client: I've been having a really hard time since losing my partner in the accident six months ago. Things I used to love, like hiking or even just watching movies on a Friday night, they feel completely hollow now, like I'm just going through the motions. I honestly wasn't sure about coming here today because I don't know if talking to someone can really fix something like this.
therapist: It takes real courage to show up today, especially when you're carrying something this heavy and feeling uncertain about whether it will even help — that doubt makes complete sense given what you've been through. The hollowness you're describing in things you once loved is such a painful and common part of grief; it doesn't mean those things are gone forever, just that your heart is still deep in mourning. I'm really glad you gave this a chance today, and I want to go at whatever pace feels right for you — can you tell me a little about what a typical day looks like for you right now?

client: A typical day is pretty bleak, honestly. I wake up and there's this split second where everything feels normal, and then it all comes crashing back, and I just kind of drag myself through work and come home to an empty apartment. I've stopped cooking real meals, I mostly just eat whatever requires no effort, and by the time evening comes I'm just staring at my phone trying to avoid the silence.
therapist: That split second of normalcy followed by the crash sounds absolutely exhausting — like losing them again, every single morning, and then having to carry that weight through an entire day. The way you're describing things — the minimal eating, avoiding the silence, just getting through — tells me you're doing the hardest possible thing right now, which is surviving, and that genuinely takes more strength than it might feel like from the inside. I'm curious about that silence you're trying to avoid in the evenings — what does it feel like it holds for you?

client: The silence feels like it's full of everything we were supposed to do together, if that makes sense. Like there are all these plans and conversations that just never got to happen, and in the quiet I can almost hear the absence of them. It sounds strange to say out loud, but sometimes I think avoiding the silence is also about avoiding how guilty I feel, because the last time we spoke we had an argument and I never got to fix it.
therapist: That doesn't sound strange at all — it sounds like one of the most human things a person can feel, and I'm really grateful you trusted me with something so tender and private. That guilt you're carrying, the weight of an unfinished conversation, is one of the most painful parts of sudden loss, but I want to gently ask you something: if the roles were reversed, and your partner was the one who survived after an argument with you, what would you want them to believe about how much you loved them?

client: I know what you're getting at, and part of me understands the logic of it, but it doesn't quite land the way I think you want it to. Because I know I would have wanted them to forgive themselves, but knowing that doesn't make me feel any less responsible for how things ended between us that day. It's like there's a gap between what I know in my head and what I actually feel, and I don't know how to close it.
therapist: You've just described something really important and insightful — that gap between what we *know* and what we *feel* is real, and it's not a flaw in your thinking or a sign that logic just needs to try harder; it means the emotional part of you hasn't been heard yet, only reasoned with. Rather than trying to close that gap by convincing yourself of something, I wonder if it might help to gently explore what that guilt is actually telling you — almost like it's a part of you that's still trying to protect the relationship, still trying to matter to them. What do you think that guilt might be holding onto that it's not quite ready to let go of?

client: That's actually a really hard question to sit with, because I think the guilt is holding onto the idea that as long as I feel bad about it, I'm still somehow in a relationship with them, still accountable to them. Like letting go of the guilt might feel like letting go of them, or admitting that what happened is just permanently unresolved and I have to live with that. And I'm not sure I'm ready for either of those things.
therapist: What you just uncovered about yourself is genuinely profound — that the guilt has become a way of staying connected, of keeping the relationship alive, and that makes it feel precious even though it's also causing you so much pain. I want you to know that letting go of guilt doesn't have to mean letting go of them — love, accountability, and connection can be carried forward in ways that don't require you to keep punishing yourself. I'm wondering, outside of the guilt, what are some of the other ways you already carry them with you each day?

client: That question actually caught me off guard in a good way, because I don't think anyone has asked me that before. I still make coffee the way they taught me, this specific way with the ratio and the timing, and I find myself noticing things on walks that I know they would have pointed out and said something funny about. But even saying that out loud makes me feel a strange mix of warmth and sadness, because it's a reminder that those small moments of carrying them are already there, and I've been so buried in the guilt that I almost couldn't see them.
therapist: What you just described — the coffee ritual, the noticing on walks — those are beautiful, living expressions of love that exist completely separately from the argument, and they've been there all along, quietly keeping the connection alive even while the guilt was demanding all your attention. That mix of warmth and sadness you're feeling right now is actually a really healthy sign; it means you're starting to touch the grief itself rather than just the guilt that's been standing in front of it. I'm curious — when you notice one of those moments, like spotting something on a walk they would have commented on, what would it feel like to let yourself pause and actually be in that moment with them, even just for a few seconds?

client: I think it could feel meaningful, but I'm also a little afraid that if I let myself fully pause and be in those moments, it might just make the loss hit harder rather than feel like connection. There's something about keeping busy and moving through those moments quickly that feels safer, even if I know on some level it's also keeping me more isolated. I guess I worry that if I open that door even a little, I won't be able to handle what comes through it.
therapist: That fear makes complete sense — you've been managing something enormous, and the strategies you've built to stay functional are there for a reason, so of course opening a door feels risky when you don't know what's on the other side. But I want to reflect something back to you: you've already opened that door a little today, right here in this conversation, and something came through — the coffee, the walks, that mix of warmth and sadness — and you're still here, still breathing, still making sense of it. I wonder, when you imagine "not being able to handle it," what does that actually look like to you — what are you most afraid would happen?

client: I think what I'm most afraid of is just completely falling apart, like losing the ability to function at work or get out of bed, and then having nobody there to help me put myself back together. I live alone now and that's the part that terrifies me the most, that I could open up all of that grief and then just be sitting in it by myself with no one to call. You're right that I got through today, but this feels like a contained space, and out there it's just me.
therapist: What you're naming - the fear of falling apart in an uncontained space with no one to catch you - is not just an anxiety, it's a real and practical concern about your support system, and it deserves to be taken seriously rather than just reassured away. You've shown today that you have tremendous insight and resilience, but resilience doesn't mean doing it alone, and part of what I'd love for us to work on together is building some of those "people to call" back into your life so that opening up doesn't have to mean being stranded in it. I'm wondering — is there anyone, even one person from before, who has reached out or who you've been keeping at a distance since the accident that some small part of you misses having around?

client: There's my friend Dara who has texted me probably a dozen times since the accident and I keep giving these short, closed-off replies that basically signal I don't want to talk. Part of me does miss her, genuinely, but I've been telling myself that being around people who knew us as a couple would just make everything worse, like I'd have to perform being okay or else deal with their discomfort about not knowing what to say. I guess I'm not sure if reaching out to her would actually feel like connection or just another thing I have to manage.
therapist: It's really telling that Dara has reached out a dozen times — that's someone who is willing to sit in the discomfort of not knowing what to say, and still keeps showing up, which suggests you might not have to perform "okay" with her as much as you fear. I also want to gently notice the thought you've built around this — that reaching out would mean *managing* her feelings — because that's actually you taking on a lot of responsibility for something that hasn't happened yet, and it might be worth testing whether that's really true. What do you think Dara would actually do if you sent her one honest message — not performing okay, but just saying something real, even something as simple as "I'm not doing well and I miss you"?

client: Honestly, I think Dara would probably respond really quickly and want to come over or call, which is actually what scares me because I don't know if I'm ready for that level of presence. But I can hear that you're right about me preemptively managing something that hasn't happened yet, and I do that a lot, I plan for the worst version of things so I can justify avoiding them. I'm not saying I'll definitely do it, but I'm not completely ruling it out either, which is probably more than I would have said an hour ago.
therapist: "Not completely ruling it out" is genuinely meaningful progress, especially for someone who walked in today unsure whether talking could help anything at all — that shift matters, even if it feels small. You've also just identified something really important about yourself, that pattern of pre-planning for the worst outcome as a way to justify staying safe, and simply *seeing* that pattern clearly is often the first step to having a choice about it. I'm wondering, if reaching out to Dara feels like too big a step right now, is there a smaller version of it — maybe not "come over" but just one honest sentence — that might feel like something you could actually try before we meet again?
